extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and literary critics (English-language, early 18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and critical guidance on composing sublime epic poetry, theatrical prologues/epilogues, and realistic portraiture of characters; includes norms about imitation, imagery, diction, audience adaptation, and moral characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of celebrated authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Should imitate the most celebrated Authors who have gone before him; e.g., if writing on a poetical Subject, consider how Homer would have spoken on such an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation lets one great Genius catch the Flame from another and write in his Spirit without copying servilely. Examples: many shining Passages in Virgil are lighted up by Homer; Milton raised and ennobled his Conceptions by imitating Longinus. Anti-pattern: slavish copying rather than assimilating spirit and adapting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scriptural and prophetic allusions in sacred subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject is sacred (Creation, etc.), make use of glorious strokes of Poetry from Holy Writ and appropriate prophetic imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select those scriptural passages that are proper for the poem and qualify high strains to fit your work. Longinus praised the sublimity of Genesis' description of Creation; Milton alludes to such texts (e.g., 'measuring the Waters in the Hollow of his Hand'). Avoid random or inappropriate citation—choose allusions that naturally suit the poem's scope and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt high strains to readers' imaginations
rubrics_metrics.description: Duly qualify high strains of Eastern/foreign poetry so they suit the Imagination of the intended readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some elevated modes of expression are suited to readers 'whose Imaginations were set to an higher pitch than those of colder Climates.' Adjust intensity and ornamentation so readers can apprehend and be moved by the sublime without alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasting modes of sublimity (tumult vs calm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different books/pieces may represent Greatness differently—e.g., one book may represent it in Confusion (like a troubled Ocean), another like the Ocean in a Calm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary the emotional texture and mode of sublimity to produce distinct effects: tumultuous, agitated description for scenes of chaos; calm, expansive description to awe the imagination without tumult. Employ the appropriate mode for the scene's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothe abstract ideas in allegory and sensible images
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry delights in cloathing abstracted Ideas in Allegories and sensible Images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn abstract theological or philosophical concepts into concrete, sensible imagery (e.g., the Divine Geometrician with golden compasses). Use allegory and tangible symbols to make high ideas accessible and poetically resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor noble, natural imagery drawn from epic tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ grand, traditional epic conceits and instruments (e.g., Golden Compasses, Minerva's Ægis) that feel natural to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose images consonant with classical tradition when they fit—these lend dignity and continuity (Homeric/Platonic echoes). Example: the 'Golden Compasses' as a natural instrument for the Almighty measurer. Anti-pattern: forcing images that feel modern or trivial into epic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness combined with vivid particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be concise enough to compress large actions (e.g., the six Days) into an episode, yet particular enough to give a lively idea of each scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance scope and detail: compress narrative breadth without losing striking particulars that make each scene vivid. Example: Milton compresses the six Days into an episode but still gives lively descriptions of the mountains, seas, and vegetation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dense, energetic diction and frequent beautie(s) of description
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy the full energy of language; lay beauties of description thickly throughout important passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply vigorous, sonorous, and richly imagistic language across descriptive passages to sustain the sublime (the poet 'employ'd on them the whole Energy of our Tongue'). Avoid weak, dilute phrasing in scenes meant to awe; do not sparsely distribute ornament where sustained grandeur is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create immersive scenes that make the reader feel present
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose descriptions so the reader seems present among the actors/spectators of the scene (e.g., 'the Reader seems present...and to assist among the Choirs of Angels').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use procession, sensory detail, and dynamic staging (gates opening, harmonies, celestial equipage) to immerse readers. The goal is a theatrical vividness—readers should feel they witness the creation rather than merely hear about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity in epilogues: arise from the play's occurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: An Epilogue should not be generic or interchangeable; it should 'wholly rise out of the Occurrences of the Piece it was composed for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write epilogues tied to the play's events and characters rather than portable, catch-all pieces. Example: defend epilogues that are felicitously connected to their play; anti-pattern: epilogues that 'might serve for any other Play.' Specificity increases relevance and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue may be gay after a tragedy when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A merry epilogue after a serious play can be proper and well received (as on the French stage, where a 'Petite Piece' follows tragedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider national/theatrical practice and audience mood: in some traditions the audience expects a lighter closure to dispel intense emotions. Example: Mrs. Oldfield's epilogue repeatedly called for and applauded. Use gaiety to send the audience home in good humour, provided it fits the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tacking comic material while passions are still flowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacking a comic tail to a tragic head can 'break the Tide of the Passions while they are yet flowing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about inserting comic relief before the audience's emotional engagement has run its course; it can dissipate powerful feelings. It may be acceptable only when the passions have already had their 'full Course.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat prologue and epilogue as distinct performances on the British stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue and Epilogue were real parts of ancient tragedy, but on the British stage they are 'distinct Performances by themselves, Pieces entirely detached from the Play, and no way essential to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose these pieces with their own dramatic logic and entertainment value; they can be independent and need not always mimic the play's tone. Understand their role and audience expectations in your theatrical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray great persons with modesty and public-spirited emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble mind should bear great Qualities without showing Consciousness of superiority; value oneself only for public spirit, justice, and integrity, and employ talents for others' use and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize heroes so their greatness appears through action and service rather than boastful display. Avoid depicting admired figures as vain, ostentatious, or seeking applause—such traits turn admiration into contempt. Example: Prince Eugene presented as modest despite heroic exploits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combined physical and behavioral detail for credible portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective portraits name stature, mien, aspect, eye, action, address, composure, and the art of mixing with company to show character (e.g., grace, vigilance, ease of address).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjoin bodily features with manner and behaviour to convey inner qualities: height for grace and agility, an erect aspect for composure, a vigilant eye for thoughtfulness. Show how comportment in public and in danger reveals character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict women's character through domestic duties and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Woman's character is contained in domestic Life; she is blameable or praiseworthy according to her carriage toward father or husband and the duties of daughter, sister, wife, and mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing female characters in the social norms the essay prescribes, foreground domestic virtues, modest dress, and moderate wit. Anti-pattern: making a woman's ambition hinge on public fame or fashions that will fade with youth and fortune; this leads to decline or derision. (This is a prescriptive social-literary guideline of the piece.)
